phonemes.desc: Short [klɛ], the unstressed first syllable of the Latin word.
Short [mɛn], the stressed second syllable of the name.
Short [ti.a], the abstract-noun ending that gives clementia its meaning.

pronunciation.approximation: 'kleh-MEN-tee-ah' — stress the second syllable; all vowels are short in Classical Latin.

kin.label: Latin root
kin.form: clemens (gen. clementis), 'mild, gentle, merciful' — the adjective behind the abstract noun; its own etymology is uncertain (de Vaan), fitting a virtue older than its name

pronunciation.note: Clementia is a Latin word and concept. It has no 'original script' other than the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form clementia is already the Latin spelling; the restoration capitalises the proper-noun form. Because no distinctive diacritic or special letter is added, the entry is Tier 2.

domains.title: Mercy and Clemency
domains.subtitle: The Virtue of Restrained Power
domains.lead: Clementia is the Roman personification and virtue of mercy, mildness, and clemency. She represents the deliberate restraint of power: the emperor who pardons a defeated enemy, the judge who tempers justice with compassion, the victor who refuses to humiliate the vanquished. In a culture that valued severity and strength, Clementia named the rare and admirable quality of showing mercy without weakness.

cards.name: Mercy
cards.desc: The willingness to spare those who have done wrong or been defeated.

cards.name: Clemency
cards.desc: The moderation of punishment by those who have the power to punish severely.

cards.name: Forgiveness
cards.desc: The release of a debtor or offender from the full weight of their debt.

cards.name: Restrained Power
cards.desc: The distinctive Roman idea that mercy is most virtuous when power is greatest.

symbols.name: Olive branch
symbols.meaning: The universal sign of peace and the offer of mercy.

symbols.name: Patera
symbols.meaning: The sacrificial bowl from which mercy is poured as a libation.

symbols.name: Kneeling suppliant
symbols.meaning: The figure who receives clemency, emphasising the power differential mercy bridges.

symbols.name: Cornucopia
symbols.meaning: The abundance that flows from a rule that is just but not cruel.

mythology.lead: Clementia is not a narrative goddess with a family tree of myths; she is a personified virtue whose 'mythology' is the history of Roman political ethics. Her story is told in senatorial debates, imperial propaganda, and the coins on which emperors advertised their mercy to the empire.

myths.title: The Clemency of Caesar
myths.text: Julius Caesar made clementia the signature of his dictatorship. Through the civil war of 49–45 BCE he pardoned one defeated enemy after another — Cicero, Ligarius, the consular Marcellus, and at last Brutus and Cassius themselves, whom he admitted to office. Cicero's speeches Pro Marcello and Pro Ligario are long acts of thanks to the quality, and the senate voted Caesar a temple of Clementia — a shrine of the goddess whose image would be the dictator's own statue, a dedication Cassius Dio (44.6) records with evident unease. The unease was the point. In a republic, clemency is a kingly gesture: only absolute power can forgive absolutely, so every pardon advertised both Caesar's mercy and the death of the old constitution. Cato chose suicide over receiving it; the Liberators, who owed their lives to it, made it their excuse. Clementia's first 'myth' is therefore double: the virtue by which Caesar conquered hearts, and — his enemies said — the crime by which he conquered Rome.

myths.title: Clementia Augusti
myths.text: The emperors inherited the gesture and made it a system. Under Nero the mint of Rome struck sestertii and dupondii showing Clementia as a standing woman, patera in hand, pouring a libation over an altar — legend CLEMENTIA AVGVSTI — and the type recurs across the coinage of the first two centuries. Imperial ideology gathered such personifications into an official register of virtues — Iustitia, Pietas, Victoria, Pax — with Clementia in the first rank; Rufus Fears's classic study mapped the whole series. The message was calibrated: the emperor is strong enough to destroy his enemies and chooses not to; the hand that could sign death warrants holds instead a sacrificial bowl. Pliny's Panegyricus would later measure every good emperor by the standard — Trajan's clementia proved, in that rhetoric, the principate's legitimacy better than any triumph. The goddess had no adventure myths of her own because she did not need them: her entire biography was minted, year by year, in bronze, and spent into every province.

myths.title: A Mirror Held to Nero
myths.text: About 55–56 CE Seneca addressed his treatise De Clementia to the nineteen-year-old Nero, and it remains the deepest text ever written on the subject. Clementia, Seneca defines, is the tempering of the mind when it has power to avenge — a virtue available only to the strong, and therefore the most regal of all (2.3). It must be distinguished from misericordia, pity: pity is a weakness of mind that succumbs to another's tears, while clemency decides by reason (2.4–6). The state is the emperor's body, and his soul its health: if the ruler is clement, mercy flows down through every magistrate and every court (1.7). History has enjoyed the irony — Nero's reign would end in matricide and terror — but the treatise outlived its dedicatee as a classic of political ethics, copied through the Middle Ages and pressed into service by every generation that has asked what mercy owes to power, and power to mercy. Seneca's definitions still govern the dictionaries.

myths.title: Mercy Becomes Divine
myths.text: Christian Latin found in clementia a ready-made name for the unearned mercy of God toward sinners, and the word passed into the liturgy where it still sounds: the Salve Regina addresses the Virgin as 'O clemens, O pia, O dulcis Virgo Maria.' The shift was a quiet revolution in the virtue's sociology. Roman clementia flowed downward from power — the victor sparing the vanquished, the master forgiving the slave, the emperor over the senate; Christian clementia Dei flows from the omnipotent toward the powerless, with no security of empire at stake, only the scandal of grace. The name Clement, borne by a first-century pope and by many successors, carried the word into the succession of Peter. Modern legal English still speaks of executive clemency — the last precinct of the goddess's domain — though no modern state dares to mint her image. She survives in the doctrine, not the statue.

lore.syncretism: The Roman Clementia overlaps with Greek Praotes (gentleness) and Eleos (mercy). She also resembles the Christian virtue of misericordia. In political theory, the concept of clemency runs from Seneca through Machiavelli — who warned princes that mercy could be dangerous — to modern discussions of presidential pardons and transitional justice. The word 'clemency' survives in legal English, though the personified goddess has faded from public memory.
lore.culturalLegacy: Clementia remains a living concept in law and politics. Executive clemency, the power to pardon or commute sentences, is one of the oldest prerogatives of rulers. The debate Seneca began — whether mercy strengthens or weakens authority — still shapes arguments about criminal justice, amnesty, and political reconciliation. In an age of mass incarceration and polarised politics, Clementia asks whether the powerful can afford to be merciful and whether the powerless can afford to hope for mercy.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Clementia is the virtue of those who have power and choose not to use all of it. That choice is harder than it sounds, because power tends to justify its own extremes. To show mercy is to acknowledge that the person before you is more than their offence, more than their defeat, more than their debt.

Yet Clementia is not sentimental. Seneca knew that mercy must be guided by justice, or it becomes licence. The ideal is not softness but strength directed toward the common good. In a world that often mistakes cruelty for clarity, Clementia reminds us that restraint can be the deepest form of power.
lore.originalScriptNote: Clementia is a Latin word. Its canonical form is the Latin spelling clementia. The ASCII form clementia already represents the Latin spelling exactly. The restoration Clementia is therefore the capitalised proper-noun citation form, not a phonetic recovery. The appropriate label is 'Latin' or 'Scholarly Transliteration'.

lore.archaeology: Clementia's monuments are numismatic above all. Nero's sestertii and dupondii of 64–66 CE show her standing with patera and cornucopia before a lighted altar, legend CLEMENTIA AVGVSTI S C, among the most beautiful personifications on Roman coinage; later emperors revived the type whenever they needed the message. In stone, a Temple of Clementia Caesaris stood at Rome, voted by the senate in 45 BCE in Caesar's honor, with the dictator's own statue installed as the goddess's image — a shrine that was also, his enemies noted, a claim to divinity on the republic's own ground. No certain remains of the temple have been identified. Personified virtues in general crowded imperial art — on the Ara Pacis, in the Forum of Nerva, on gems and cameos — but Clementia's own dossier is bronze and silver: the empire's most widely circulated theology.
